summary: Defines an extension to the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) that lets a modem report the range of latency that can be experienced on a link, rather than just a single value.

eli5.summary: A bus company says a trip takes between 10 and 20 minutes instead of one number. This lets a radio link tell a router how long delays might be.

questions: what is the dlep latency range extension
subtitle: A DLEP extension that reports minimum and maximum link latency instead of a single value.

tldr.problem: The base Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Latency Data Item gives only one implementation-dependent latency value for a link.
tldr.mechanism: A Latency Range extension (Extension Type Value 4) adds a Latency Range Data Item (type 28) carrying a 64-bit maximum and a 64-bit minimum latency in microseconds.
tldr.outcome: Routers can learn the range of delay seen on a link. Use of the extension SHOULD be configurable.

today: RFC 8757 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Range Instead of One Number
sections.content:
DLEP (RFC 8175) exchanges link control information between a modem and a router. It supports extensions, and this document defines one, called Latency Range.

The base specification has a Latency Data Item with a single latency value. This extension adds the minimum and maximum latency seen on a link.
sections.eli5: The old way gave one number for delay. The new way gives the shortest and the longest.

sections.title: Turning the Extension On
sections.content:
Use of the extension SHOULD be configurable. To use it, an implementation MUST include the Latency Range Extension Type Value, which is 4, in the Extensions Supported Data Item, which is handled as in RFC 8175.

Using the extension does not change how the base Latency Data Item is processed.
sections.eli5: Both sides announce that they speak this extra feature, and the old way of reporting still works.

sections.title: The Latency Range Data Item
sections.content:
The Latency Range Data Item MUST be included in the Session Initialization Response Message, with default values used session-wide. It MAY also appear in any message where the Latency Data Item is allowed, as an additional data item, and is processed by the same rules.

Its Data Item Type is 28 and its Length is 16. It holds a 64-bit unsigned Maximum Latency, the longest delay a packet encounters on the link, followed by a 64-bit unsigned Minimum Latency, the shortest delay a packet can encounter. Both are in microseconds.
sections.eli5: It is a small note with two numbers: the longest wait and the shortest wait for a message to cross the link.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The extension adds no vulnerabilities beyond those in RFC 8175, and that document's approach to security applies. IANA assigned Extension Type Value 4 and Data Item Type 28, both named Latency Range.
sections.eli5: The extra note adds no new risks, and it got its own official numbers.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the data item value.

fields.name: Maximum Latency
fields.desc: Longest transmission delay a packet encounters, in microseconds.

fields.name: Minimum Latency
fields.desc: Shortest transmission delay a packet can encounter, in microseconds.

references.text: Ratliff, S., Jury, S., Satterwhite, D., Taylor, R., and B. Berry, "Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP)", RFC 8175, June 2017.
